description: TecMedHub: applied science lab from Universidad Austral de Chile (Puerto Montt). We solve real problems with technology, from the south. We bring AI and computer vision, 3D printing/CNC, augmented reality and prototyping, all open source. Looking for: data scientists (satellite/remote sensing data), Python/JS developers, UI/UX designers and storytellers. Curious minds from any field welcome. Spanish/English. tecmedhub.org
summary: PuduHealth is an open health-monitoring platform for long-duration space missions. Any medical sensor, our own designs or third-party devices, sends measurements through one open API (puduhealth/v1), and the platform compares each astronaut with their own baseline instead of a population limit. On real Fitbit data from 14 people, the personal detector flags a sustained +5 bpm rise in 3 days (median) while alerting on only 2.5 % of ordinary days. Every alert tells the astronaut what to do and when to call the crew medical officer, and cites its source (NASA-STD-3001, OCHMO technical briefs). A trained acute-stress model (AUC 0.93 on WESAD ECG) runs on the phone with heart rate from any sensor. Data stays on the device, encrypted, because astronauts tend to under-report symptoms for fear of losing future flights (Institute of Medicine 2001; NASA OCHMO-TB-014), and the app works offline, even when the Sun blocks communication with Mars. It is an installable phone app in English and Spanish, with an example Mars mission that replays the radiation Curiosity's RAD instrument measured. We built it in Quemchi, Chiloé, where rural health posts face the same question: is this normal for this person, and when do I call?
details:
What it does

PuduHealth is an open health-monitoring platform for long-duration missions. Any source of measurements, our own sensor designs, third-party medical devices, onboard equipment or the astronaut's daily check-in, delivers them through one open API in a single format (puduhealth/v1). The platform compares each astronaut with their own baseline, flags a sustained drift long before a standard's red line, and tells the person who has to act what to do and when to call the crew medical officer, citing the source of every recommendation. The phone camera is only a fallback adapter we built because we had no hardware: hardware can change without touching the engine.

How it works

  • Connect: measurements arrive through the in-page API (window.puduHealth.registrar), JSON/CSV import from a device, or the camera adapter. Units are checked, so a wrong unit is rejected instead of stored. Standard Bluetooth profiles (Heart Rate, Health Thermometer) and our ESP32 wearable are designed, not built yet.
  • Estimate: a personal baseline per variable (mean, standard deviation, z-score and an EWMA trend), calibrated on real data (PMData, 14 people, ~5 months: 2.5 % of days with a heart-rate alert; a sustained +5 bpm rise caught in 3 days). In My record, the first 7 days calibrate the baseline. A trained acute-stress model (logistic regression, AUC 0.93 leaving one person out on WESAD ECG) runs on the phone with heart rate from any sensor.
  • Decide: 14 deterministic rules with cited thresholds (NASA-STD-3001, OCHMO TB-020/030/031, AASM/SRS, PHQ-9) give a traffic light for five NASA HRP risks: cardiovascular, bone and muscle, behavioral, immune and radiation. A missing value is never treated as zero.
  • Act: each alert gives the action and its source; a clear clinical screen, without the companion, says when to contact the medical officer.

Benefits and intended impact

Fixed limits warn late. In a simulated mission where we scripted a decline (less sleep and training from day 135), the commander's first personal warnings arrive 55 days before NASA's VO2max limit; this illustrates the mechanism, it is not a measurement. In Chiloé, the Navy patrol ship Cirujano Videla brings doctors and health teams to the islands on medical rounds; on the way to Mars there is no interplanetary Cirujano Videla, so the crew and its medical officer, with the medical equipment on board, must decide without Earth. Astronauts tend to under-report symptoms for fear of losing future flights (Institute of Medicine, Safe Passage, 2001, ch. 6 p. 174; NASA OCHMO-TB-014, 2023), so answers never leave the device: AES-256 encryption, optional PIN, no server, accounts or analytics. Everything runs on board and offline, including the two weeks every two years when the Sun blocks communication with Mars. We built it in Quemchi, Chiloé, where rural health posts are run by paramedic technicians and doctors arrive by sea: the same engine with another rule set could support them (a direction we have not tested yet).

Creativity

A platform, not a sensor. Each person is their own reference. Privacy is treated as a health measure, not only a policy. Astropudú, an astronaut pudú (the world's smallest deer, native to Chiloé), rewards habits and never judges feelings. The example crew lives, day by day, the radiation Curiosity's RAD instrument measured on its way to Mars and on the surface.

Tools

HTML, CSS and JavaScript (ES modules, no framework, no backend); Web Crypto (AES-GCM, PBKDF2); web app manifest and service worker (installable, offline); Python (pandas, scikit-learn) and Node.js for calibration, training and evaluation; ffmpeg and headless Chromium to record the video from the real app; edge-tts for the narration; PHP for the pulse-meter prototype used to collect our recordings; GitHub Pages for hosting. 64 automated tests.

Factors we considered

Personal data protection (on-device encryption, pseudonymous participant codes and informed consent in our own study, Chile Laws 19.628/21.719/20.584, GDPR Articles 9 and 25); honesty about what is real and what is simulated; missing data; offline use; Spanish and English; accessibility. It is a hackathon prototype, not a medical device, and not clinically validated.

Links

  • App (installable): tecmedhub.github.io/puduhealth/app
  • Presentation (7 slides, live app inside): tecmedhub.github.io/puduhealth/pitch
  • Project site and videos (English and Spanish, 16:9 and 9:16): tecmedhub.github.io/puduhealth
  • API documentation: github.com/TecMedHub/puduhealth/wiki

Use of AI

Code and documentation were written with an AI coding assistant (Claude, by Anthropic) and reviewed and tested by the team; AI also helped search and check sources and translate the docs. The video narration uses synthetic AI voices (Microsoft neural TTS via edge-tts), shown on screen and in the video metadata. The Astropudú illustration was AI-generated from the team's own design and is marked "AI-generated art". The soundtrack is original music by team member Benjamín Catipillan-Ulloa. No NASA logos or branding are used.
